10.1175/jtech-d-26-0075.1.t: Improved Significant Wave Height Retrieval from SAR Imagery in Tropical Cyclones Using Wind-Context Proxies
10.1175/jtech-d-26-0075.1.j: Journal of Atmospheric and Oceanic Technology
10.1175/jtech-d-26-0075.1.a: Abstract Accurate retrieval of significant wave height (SWH) under tropical cyclone (TC) conditions is essential for marine hazard warning and ocean dynamics studies. Although spaceborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) offers unique capabilities for observing extreme sea states, existing empirical wave retrieval models often do not fully account for TC wind context. This study presents CWAVE_S1TC, a wind-context-based extension of the CWAVE model, which incorporates three key proxies of TC wind context derived from SAR wind retrievals: the local surface wind speed, the maximum wind speed, and the normalized radial distance, to enhance SWH retrieval. A dataset comprising 63 Sentinel-1 SAR scenes from 40 TC events, together with collocated reference SWH from the ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis and WAVEWATCH III hindcast data, is used for model development and validation. The three proxies show significant correlations with SWH, with correlation coefficients of 0.84, 0.56, and −0.49, respectively. CWAVE_S1TC achieves a coefficient of determination of 0.81 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.03 m, outperforming the basic CWAVE_S1 model in the model-development dataset. Independent validation against WW3 data shows that CWAVE_S1TC reduces the Bias from 0.61 m to 0.37 m and the RMSE from 1.86 m to 1.14 m, while increasing the correlation coefficient from 0.77 to 0.85. Leave-one-storm-out and cross-basin validation further demonstrate model robustness and applicability beyond the model-development region. These results highlight the value of incorporating TC wind-context information into SAR-based SWH retrieval and demonstrate the potential of CWAVE_S1TC for improving SWH retrieval under TC conditions.

10.3389/fmars.2026.1969172.t: GLM-OOTKG: an LLM-driven framework for constructing knowledge graphs in ocean observation technology
10.3389/fmars.2026.1969172.a: Despite the accumulation of vast amounts of ocean observation data and diverse instrumentation, a critical gap persists in modern oceanography: instruments and their generated heterogeneous datasets are routinely treated as isolated entities, lacking a systematic knowledge graph to map the overarching observation technology ecosystem. This systemic disconnection creates a severe semantic gap between raw instrument specifications and the geophysical parameters they measure, ultimately hindering automated cross-platform interoperability and intelligent data discovery. To bridge this gap, we introduce GLM-OOTKG(GLM-driven Ocean Observation Technology Knowledge Graph), a Large Language Model (LLM)-based framework designed to construct a comprehensive knowledge graph for ocean observation technologies. Specifically, we propose a constraint-based prompting strategy that integrates predefined domain ontologies, few-shot examples, and explicit null-response instructions. This strategy effectively mitigates LLM hallucinations, enabling the accurate extraction of complex technical relationships among instruments, specifications, and variables from unstructured literature. Furthermore, we develop a dual-weighted ranking algorithm built upon Transformer embeddings to reconcile terminological inconsistencies and achieve precise entity alignment across heterogeneous documents. Evaluated on a curated corpus of oceanographic technical literature, GLM-OOTKG achieves F1-scores of 88.9% in entity extraction and 87.0% in relationship extraction, significantly outperforming unconstrained baselines by absolute margins of 9.0% and 13.4%, respectively. Ultimately, the resulting knowledge graph serves as a robust semantic bridge between observation hardware and derived data products, providing a structured, machine-readable metadata foundation that conceptually supports future downstream tasks, such as multi-source data assimilation and cross-platform synergies within the Space–Air–Ground–Ocean observation network.

10.1080/1755876x.2026.2742732.t: Forecast skill of the INCOIS operational ocean general circulation models – case study for 2020
10.1080/1755876x.2026.2742732.a: The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) provides daily 7-day ocean forecasts for the Indian Ocean as a part of Regional Integrated Multi-Hazard Early Warning System (RIMES) initiative using ROMS and HYCOM models. This study validates first-day forecasts of sea surface temperature (SST) and currents for 2020 against moored buoy data, satellite observations, and analysis products, applying Allan-Murphy’s forecast verification framework. Subsurface currents were assessed using ADCP observations. Both models captured SST variability with high spatial correlation; ROMS showed slightly better SST skill. HYCOM performed better for basin-scale surface and subsurface current forecasts, realistically reproducing mesoscale eddies and the East India Coastal Current, while buoy comparisons indicated ROMS outperformed HYCOM for local surface currents. Despite configuration differences, both systems demonstrated statistically comparable performance on first day SST and current, with discrepancies linked to unresolved processes, model physics, atmospheric forcing, and observational limitations. Skill score analysis revealed substantial value addition of SST forecasts relative to climatology, with root mean square deviation (RMSD) lower than standard deviation (STD). Current forecasts showed lower skill, with RMSD exceeding STD. Overall, the study highlights the strengths and limitations of INCOIS operational ocean forecasting systems and emphasises the importance of continuous verification to enhance prediction services across the Indian Ocean.

10.5194/os-22-3435-2026.t: Three-dimensional structure of sub-mesoscale eddies on the continental shelf
10.5194/os-22-3435-2026.a: Abstract. Sub-mesoscale eddies are oceanic features crucial for energy transfer processes, transport of heat and biogeochemical tracers, and for promoting diversity in marine ecosystems. Their small length scales (<20 km) and short lifespans (O~days), make their characterization challenging using field measurements. In this paper, we combined remote sensing, ocean glider, shipborne, and mooring data to investigate the internal structure and dynamical properties of sub-mesoscale eddies and peddies ('petite' eddies; diameters ≤10 km extending through the water column) along the Wadjemup (Rottnest) Continental Shelf (WCS), Western Australia. Data collected in August 2010 showed an anti-cyclonic mesoscale eddy spawning several cyclonic, cold core sub-mesoscale eddies that promoted upwelling (vertical extension ~185 m) with maxima in chlorophyll concentration at the centre. Results suggested that sub-mesoscale eddies drive chlorophyll advection either at (in) their periphery (centre) of cyclonic eddies, or at their interfaces. In general, cyclonic eddies promoted upwelling and anti-cyclonic eddies promoted downwelling; however, our data also showed that upwelling conditions could also occur in anti-cyclonic eddies. Winds were found to affect the internal structure and lifecycle of sub-mesoscale eddies, particularly under strong wind (speeds > 7 ms-1) conditions, through upwelling and/or vertical mixing. In the presence of dense shelf water outflows along the continental shelf, sub-mesoscale eddies were found to trap, upwell, and transport denser nearshore waters off the continental shelf. This unique dataset provided a detailed picture of the three-dimensional structure of sub-mesoscale eddies, including the characterization of sub-surface eddies, and contributes to the understanding of their role in chlorophyll advection in shelf and coastal environments.

10.3389/fmars.2026.1974481.t: Object-based sample augmentation improves rare-class seabed sediment mapping from multibeam data in the East Sea (Sea of Japan)
10.3389/fmars.2026.1974481.a: Seabed-sediment classification from multibeam echo-sounder data is constrained by sparse, class-imbalanced ground truth, particularly for coarse gravel, which pixel-based classifiers struggle to resolve. This study maps the seabed sediments of the southwestern East Sea (Sea of Japan) continental shelf using object-based sample augmentation, which propagates field-sample labels across Simple Linear Iterative Clustering superpixels of calibrated backscatter and bathymetry. Under 20-seed repeated random cross-validation, object-based augmentation raised the rare-class (Gravel) F1-score from 0.036 for a pixel-only baseline to 0.436, and the gain persisted under spatial-block cross-validation, a within-scene spatial-robustness test on spatially held-out sites (0.024 to 0.311), where SLIC exceeded all tested fixed-neighborhood scales. These rare-class estimates rest on only eight independent Gravel field sites and should be interpreted in that context. Oversampling the original rare-class anchors to the same training size recovered only a minority of this gain, indicating that most of the improvement arose from newly propagated pixels rather than anchor replication. Feature-space and multi-sample diagnostics provided empirical support for the within-superpixel label-propagation assumption. The resulting gravel–sand–mud map reproduces a depth-controlled, fining-offshore facies pattern consistent with hydraulic sorting on the narrow, river-fed shelf. An expert-interpreted Rock assessment further showed that exposed bedrock could not be reliably separated from coarse gravel at an acceptable trade-off in the available single-frequency-per-location backscatter–bathymetry feature space. Overall, the approach recovers rare coarse-substrate facies that pixel-based mapping largely misses while identifying the limits of acoustic-only substrate discrimination, thereby strengthening the baseline seabed-sediment maps that underpin benthic habitat mapping, marine spatial planning, and seabed engineering.

10.1029/2026gl123962.t: Detecting the Oceanic Moho Using Teleseismic P‐Wave Coda Autocorrelations of Ocean Bottom Seismograph Records
10.1029/2026gl123962.a: Abstract Although active‐source seismic methods can image the oceanic Mohorovičić discontinuity (Moho) at high resolution, their high cost motivates passive approaches using OBS, for which receiver functions (RF) are often complicated by instrument tilt, azimuthal misalignment, sedimentary layers, and water‐column reverberations. Here we apply teleseismic P‐wave coda autocorrelation to hydrophone data from OBS to image the oceanic Moho. Compared with vertical‐component data, hydrophone data provide a simpler interpretation because they avoid P‐to‐S conversions and are dominated by reflected and transmitted P‐wave energy. By analyzing autocorrelation results from 22 long‐period and 24 short‐period stations in the NoMelt experiment, we identify a Moho reflection with a TwTT of ∼2.56 s and resolve lateral variations in crustal TwTT that are smoothed out in the radially averaged representations of global velocity models. Combined with previous studies and model tests, this longer‐than‐expected crustal TwTT suggests that a crust‐mantle transition zone may exist beneath the NoMelt region.
